lines.text: Almanak decides. KeeperHub lands it. And the strategy code never changes.
Every DeFi agent framework has the same blind spot. The strategy is the interesting part. Execution is where it actually breaks.
Almanak compiles a strategy down to raw calldata, then hands it to an executor that has to sign it, broadcast it, survive a stuck nonce, and never, ever send it twice.
Almanak's execution layer is three abstract classes. A Signer, a Submitter, and a Simulator.
So I implemented all three against KeeperHub. The strategy has no idea. The only change to Almanak's own demo strategy is a single line, adding Base Sepolia to its supported chains.
Now every transaction the strategy plans goes through KeeperHub's enclave wallet, its spending caps, its simulation, and its audit log. Gas is sponsored. The private key never touches my process.
Here it is running on Base Sepolia. A real strategy tick, a real approve, a real deposit, verified on chain.
The strategy plans an approve and a deposit. Both are dry-run through KeeperHub first, then broadcast through it.
Both land. Both come back verified, with KeeperHub's relayer paying the gas, so the organization wallet never needs a native balance.
The same run is visible in the local console, in the KeeperHub dashboard, and from a Telegram bot on my phone. Let me show you the phone.
The same backend, from a phone. The Telegram bot is the operator's view: the same receipts and the same commands, and nothing it can do that the command line cannot.
Status. The chain, the organisation wallet, and the counts. The key is in KeeperHub's enclave. There is no key on the phone, and none on the laptop either.
Every execution, with its KeeperHub id and a link to the explorer.
Verify asks KeeperHub for its verdict on one hash, then reads the receipt. The transaction sender is the sponsor's paymaster. The events name the organisation wallet as the one that acted.
A dry run. Almanak plans the tick, KeeperHub simulates it. Nothing is signed.
A real tick needs a confirmation. Almanak plans, KeeperHub dry-runs, then signs inside its enclave and broadcasts.
The alerts arrive as it happens. Approve broadcast, deposit broadcast, both settled, both verified.
Then a stale decision: redeem one share more than the wallet holds. KeeperHub reads the balance itself before acting, five million, not enough, and refuses. Nothing is broadcast.

And the exit. Almanak decides to redeem; the order goes out as KeeperHub's check-and-execute. KeeperHub reads the vault balance itself right before the write, sees the five million shares, and only then redeems. The test USDC comes back.
And the duplicate. The same intent sent twice. KeeperHub replays the first execution instead of sending again. One transaction on chain.
But an execution backend is judged on what it does when things go wrong. So I built seven failure modes on purpose and recorded every one.
An unknown selector is refused before anything is signed. A call that would revert is caught by the dry run. A duplicate is blocked by an idempotency key bound to the intent, not to the attempt.
And when the process is killed in the middle of a bundle, it resumes from the receipts log, and never broadcasts the same transaction twice.

Fifty out of fifty impossible deposits refused before broadcast. Two hundred out of two hundred executions landed and verified, median seven point eight seconds. Fifty out of fifty retries replayed, zero double broadcasts. Ten out of ten crashed processes resumed.

Five hundred and sixty tests, eleven of them run against production every six hours by a workflow that also runs a real tick and republishes the proof. And three issues filed against KeeperHub itself, all three accepted, two already merged.
Almanak strategies, executed by KeeperHub. No strategy code changes.
